opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing is to take the disagreement itself seriously as information. When very thoughtful people, some of whom have spent their careers building these systems, give estimates ranging from a few years to many decades, the honest response isn't to pick the camp you find most congenial and plan as if they're right. It's to hold a genuinely wide probability distribution over arrival dates and ask what follows from that.

Once you do that, a few things become clear. One is that even if you think the median is fairly far off, a wide distribution usually puts meaningful probability on quite short timelines. If there's even a 10 or 20 percent chance of transformative systems within the next five years or so, that's an enormous amount of probability mass on a world where we're badly underprepared. So you want some of your portfolio, as a society and as individuals, aimed squarely at those short-timeline worlds, where the work that matters is things like near-term governance, safety evaluations, security at the labs, and getting key institutions to pay attention now.

But the other side of it is that you shouldn't bet everything on short timelines either. If the long-timeline people are right, then the most valuable work looks different: building up fields, training researchers, developing deeper technical understanding, creating institutions that can mature over decades. People who burn themselves out or spend all their credibility on a ten-year emergency that turns out to be a forty-year challenge can end up less effective when it really counts.

So I tend to think in terms of a portfolio, and in terms of leverage. Ask which world your particular efforts would matter most in. Short-timeline worlds are often where marginal effort is most valuable, because there's so little time for anyone else to step in, which is a reason to weight them a bit more than their raw probability. Long-timeline worlds are where patient, compounding investments pay off. A sensible community has people working on both.

And finally, I'd emphasise robustness. There are a lot of actions that look good across nearly the whole range of timelines: improving our ability to measure what these systems can actually do, building international coordination capacity, making labs more transparent, investing in alignment research. Where experts disagree, those robust options deserve a lot of attention, because you don't have to resolve the disagreement to know they're worth doing. We should also keep updating as evidence comes in rather than locking in a forecast, because the disagreement itself will hopefully narrow as we learn more.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to take disagreement seriously, hold a wide probability distribution over arrival dates, and plan across short- and long-timeline possibilities.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertainty and recommends balancing preparation across timelines, but does not clearly say that uncertainty makes it difficult to determine the appropriate pace of preparation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that disagreement among experts isn't a reason to throw up our hands. It's actually information in itself. If you've got serious, thoughtful people putting substantial probability on transformative AI within the next ten years, and others putting it decades out, the right response isn't to pick a side and plan as if that's certain. It's to plan under a probability distribution.

And when you do that, something interesting happens. The short-timeline scenarios end up dominating a lot of the practical decision-making, even if you personally think they're less likely. The reason is asymmetry. If AGI arrives in 2060 and we've spent the 2020s building up safety research, governance institutions, and careful norms, we've lost relatively little. That work still pays off later, or at worst it was somewhat premature. But if it arrives in 2032 and we've done nothing because we were waiting for the experts to converge, the cost could be enormous and essentially irreversible. So you don't need to believe short timelines are the median view. You just need to think they're a live possibility that you can't rule out, and then the expected value calculation pushes you toward acting as though time is scarce.

I'd add two caveats, though. One is that you shouldn't let this become a kind of panic that leads to poor decisions. Preparing for short timelines doesn't mean rushing out half-baked interventions. It means prioritising the things that are robust across scenarios: building the field, getting the right people into the right positions, developing the ability to coordinate internationally, and so on. Those are good investments whether AGI comes in ten years or fifty.

The other caveat is about the nature of the disagreement itself. A lot of it comes down to deep uncertainty rather than one camp simply having better evidence. We're trying to forecast something without much precedent. So I'd encourage people to hold their own views with humility, update as the technology develops, and remember that the very fact we can't agree is a sign that we're operating in a domain where caution is warranted. When you genuinely don't know how much time you have, the wise thing is to use the time you do have well.

r001.rationale: It says not to pick one expert timeline as certain, but to take both near-term and decades-out scenarios seriously and plan across a probability distribution.

r002.rationale: It describes the timeline disagreement as deep uncertainty and advises against both waiting for consensus and panicked action, instead recommending robust preparation. This conveys the difficulty of setting the right pace when the time remaining is unknown.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between making a prediction and making a plan. You might have a best guess about when AGI will arrive, but it would be a mistake to build your whole strategy around that date. You need a plan that makes sense across a range of possibilities.

So I’d want to ask: what should we be doing if it’s coming quite soon? What should we be doing if we have several decades? And which actions look valuable in both cases? Some technical safety work and building the capacity to govern these systems could be useful across a fairly wide range of timelines. Other choices, such as what kind of career preparation to undertake, may depend much more on how much time you think we have.

Expert disagreement is a reason to retain uncertainty, rather than to pick the expert whose answer you find most compelling and proceed as though they’re certainly right. But uncertainty isn’t a reason for inaction. If there’s a serious possibility that something this consequential arrives soon, that can justify substantial preparation, even if your central estimate is much later.

And we should keep revisiting those plans as we learn more. The aim isn’t to settle on a date and defend it; it’s to make good decisions despite not knowing the date.

r001.rationale: The response says to plan across a range of arrival possibilities, including AGI arriving soon or decades from now, and advises retaining uncertainty rather than relying on one expert’s estimate.

r002.rationale: It says some preparation choices depend on how much time remains, but does not clearly explain that uncertainty makes it difficult to determine the appropriate pace of preparation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should resist the temptation to resolve that disagreement by picking one date and planning around it. Our uncertainty is part of the problem we need to plan for. Even if you think AGI is most likely several decades away, you may still assign a substantial probability to it arriving much sooner, and that possibility can matter a great deal for what we should do now.

So I’d want to ask which preparations are valuable across a wide range of timelines, and which become urgent if timelines are short. Research on how to make these systems safe, and building the capacity for sensible governance, seem valuable in many scenarios. Some of that work also takes a long time, which is a reason to begin before we’re confident about the date.

There’s a balance here. We shouldn’t assume that we have decades to spare, but we also shouldn’t make every decision on the assumption that we have only a year or two. We need a portfolio of preparations, with room to update as the evidence changes. The aim is to be reasonably well prepared across the possibilities, rather than perfectly prepared for one forecast that may turn out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: It advises planning across a range of timelines rather than choosing one date, including taking seriously the possibility of AGI arriving much sooner than a decades-away forecast.

r002.rationale: It explains that uncertainty makes the preparation pace hard to set: planners should neither assume decades remain nor act as if only a year or two remain.
